extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/aesthetics; critics, writers, and artists interested in theories of taste and humor
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for assessing the aesthetic value of arts (poetry, music, painting, jokes) and an account of laughter, naiveté, genius, and the antinomy of taste. Focuses on what makes art 'beautiful' vs merely 'pleasant' and what produces comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form as essential in beautiful art
rubrics_metrics.description: In all beautiful art the essential thing is the form, which is purposive as regards our observation and judgement, where the pleasure is at the same time cultivation and disposes the spirit to Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matter of sensation (charm or emotion) pertains only to enjoyment and leaves nothing in the Idea; excessive focus on sensation makes the spirit dull and the object gradually distasteful. The aesthetic worth depends on purposive form aligning imagination with the faculty of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with moral Ideas for lasting worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Beautiful arts that are not brought into close combination with moral Ideas will ultimately serve only as distraction and fail to produce self-sufficing satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art disconnected from moral Ideas becomes mere diversion that increases the mind's discontent; combining beauty with moral Ideas supplies a deeper, enduring satisfaction ('self-sufficing satisfaction').

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's primacy among the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry maintains the first rank among the arts: it expands the mind by setting the Imagination at liberty and unites the presentation of a concept with a wealth of thought, rising aesthetically to Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry originates largely in genius (not precept), strengthens the mind by enabling free, spontaneous judgement, and 'plays with illusion' only as declared play—therefore it does not deceive. Its freedom from strict rules lets it reach higher aesthetic Ideas than other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as potentially deceitful (not aesthetic ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric, insofar as it is persuasion (the art of deceiving by a beautiful show), is a Dialectic that borrows from poetry only enough to win minds before they form judgement, and therefore is not recommendable for law or pulpit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rhetoric may be used for praiseworthy ends, its capacity to 'captivate' risks spoiling maxims and dispositions subjectively even where actions may be objectively lawful. Where lasting instruction and moral determination are at stake, plain presentation combined with eloquence is preferable to persuasive artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music (art of tone) as intense but transient enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Music moves the mind in a greater variety of ways and more intensely but is enjoyment rather than culture; in the judgement of Reason it has less worth than other beautiful arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music expresses aesthetic Ideas through tone and mathematical relations (harmony/melody), producing transitory impressions that demand constant change and do not bear frequent repetition without weariness. Music can be obtrusive (sound spreads) unlike visual arts, and thus may lack 'urbanity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Formative arts supply permanent cognitive culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative arts (e.g., painting) produce permanent products that serve as vehicles for concepts, promoting the union of sensibility and understanding and thereby carrying on a serious business of culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formative arts proceed from determinate Ideas to sensations and create durable intuitions aligned with concepts, so they have higher 'cultural' worth than arts that only stimulate sensation (like music). Painting is given special prominence for its capacity to penetrate the region of Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: satisfaction in judgement vs gratification
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between what satisfies simply in the act of judging (aesthetic satisfaction) and what gratifies (pleasure in sensation); gratification often relates to bodily well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gratification can be bodily and fleeting and may even conflict with reasoned approbation or disapprobation; aesthetic satisfaction pertains to cultivation of the mind and approbation by Reason rather than mere bodily pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three species of free play that gratify
rubrics_metrics.description: The free play of sensations that gratifies may be subdivided into (1) play of fortune (games of chance), (2) play of tone (music), and (3) play of thought (wit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games (play of fortune) require interest and alternate strong affections (hope/fear) producing bodily vivacity; music (play of tone) changes sensations linked to affection; wit (play of thought) animates the mind by changing representations without producing interest-bearing thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of laughter (what makes us laugh)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is 'an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For laughter to occur the jest must contain something capable of deceiving for a moment; the expected object must be suddenly dissipated into nothing (not transformed into a positive opposite). Examples: the Indian who wonders how ale got into a bottle; the heir who pays mourners to look sad but makes them cheerful. The momentary illusion and its abrupt collapse produce the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism for joke-induced bodily gratification
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect operates by a rapid alternating tension and relaxation of the mind's expectation that produces involuntary bodily movements (intestinal/diaphragmatic oscillation) and a feeling of bodily health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the mind is momentarily deceived and then the illusion dissipates suddenly, an inner bodily movement harmonises with mental oscillation, expelling air in bursts and producing pleasurable vivacity; this physiological rebound is central to why we laugh and find jokes gratifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of momentary deception in a successful jest
rubrics_metrics.description: In every instance that excites a convulsive laugh there must be something absurd in which the Understanding finds no satisfaction—i.e., an element that deceives briefly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story simply proves false (without creating a momentary illusion) it may displease rather than amuse. Effective jokes create a temporary, plausible tension of expectation and then dissolve it into nothing, prompting laughter rather than annoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naiveté as aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Naiveté is the breaking out of original sincerity in opposition to the art of dissimulation; we laugh at simplicity that does not dissemble and delight in the unspoiled nature that thwarts assumed manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naiveté combines seriousness and tender compassion, and while the representation of naiveté in a fictional character is possible and beautiful, an art that is truly 'naive' (i.e., produced by deliberate art) is a contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous manner defined and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is the talent to voluntarily assume a mental disposition in which everything is judged quite differently from the ordinary method (reversed, yet in accordance with rational principles); this manner belongs more to pleasant than to beautiful art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'humorous' person can adopt such frames of mind purposively (distinct from someone involuntarily 'of humours'), using contrast to excite laughter. Because the beautiful requires intrinsic worth and seriousness, purely humorous manner is not the primary mode of beautiful art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antinomy of taste (thesis vs antithesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an apparent antinomy: (Thesis) the judgement of taste is not based upon concepts (so it cannot be proved), versus (Antithesis) the judgement of taste is based on concepts (for otherwise we could not quarrel about it or claim universal assent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conflict arises from taking the relevant 'concept' in the same sense in both maxims; resolution requires distinguishing determinate concepts (of understanding) from indeterminate rational concepts (supersensible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution: taste refers to indeterminate supersensible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste refers to a concept, but not a determinate, demonstrable one; rather it refers to an indeterminate pure rational concept of the supersensible which cannot supply proof yet underlies the claim to universal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the determining ground is an undeterminable transcendent concept, taste cannot be proved by concepts of understanding (avoiding thesis) yet can claim universal validity (avoiding antithesis). This reconciles the antinomy by showing both propositions can be true in different senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between aesthetical and rational Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas are representations that cannot become cognition: aesthetical Ideas are intuitions of the Imagination (inexponible), while rational Ideas are transcendent concepts of Reason (indemonstrable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetical Ideas cannot be expounded fully by concepts because the imagination's internal intuition resists reduction to conceptual understanding; rational Ideas cannot be demonstrated because intuition corresponding to them cannot be given. These distinctions underpin discussions of taste, genius, and aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as faculty of aesthetical Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the faculty of aesthetical Ideas; in products of genius nature, not premeditated purpose, supplies the rule of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the beautiful cannot be judged by determinate concepts but by an unconditioned purposiveness of the imagination, genius provides original, exemplary works that serve as standards without being the product of explicit rules or precepts.
